narrative:
Your law school application was denied because the assessment estimated a 54% probability that you would fail the bar exam on the first attempt. That is not a certainty—about half the risk estimate points the other way—but it was high enough to cross the admissions risk threshold.

Most influential was your LSAT score. At 25.50, compared with an average of 37.18 among accepted students, it pushed the prediction most strongly toward failure.

Your undergraduate GPA was the second most influential factor. At 2.80, it counted in your favor in this prediction, pushing toward passing, but it was not enough to offset the LSAT.

Your third-year class standing was the third most influential and pushed toward failure: being in the third decile, versus an accepted-student average around the sixth decile, added to the concern.

Next, contact admissions to ask whether the decision can be reviewed and what supporting information they accept. Consider retaking the LSAT after preparation, strengthening your academic record if possible, and providing context about your GPA or class standing. Ask whether a conditional admission, waitlist, or appeal process exists. The 54% estimate should be read as a risk signal, not a final judgment of your ability.
